Research on whether children learn language skills from television yields conflicting findings. [d1] On one hand, high-credibility sources note that well-designed television programs like Sesame Street can improve cognitive, literacy, and social outcomes for children aged 3 to 5 years [d2], and a peer-reviewed study found that educational programs may be beneficial for child language development, with formats such as Sesame Street and Dora the Explorer designed to encourage verbal response and age-appropriate pacing [d7]; additionally, a study using the PBS program 'Molly of Denali' found that 1st graders who watched it showed improved ability to use informational text, suggesting educational TV can teach complex reading skills [d4]. On the other hand, a study of 275 families published in Science Daily found that TV viewing had no effect on language development—neither positive nor negative—while back-and-forth conversation was six times more influential [d12], and a separate study found that toddlers who watched the Baby Einstein DVD actually showed no improvement in language skills compared to those who did not [d11]; the American Academy of Pediatrics also warns that excessive screen time displaces opportunities for language practice and social interaction [d10]. Overall, the evidence suggests that TV can be a helpful supplementary tool for language learning when programs are high-quality, co-viewing with adults is active, and viewing is moderate in amount [d1][d2][d7], but that excessive viewing—especially unaccompanied viewing—may be more harmful to language development than beneficial [d6][d10][d12].
[[END-OF-ANSWER]]
